name: Scoliosis bracing / fusion surgery

card.summary: Established orthopaedic treatments for spinal curvature; bracing aims to halt progression in growing teens, fusion straightens severe curves.
card.note: Surgery is major; brace outcomes depend heavily on wear compliance.

quick.overview:
Scoliosis bracing and spinal fusion are medical treatments for sideways spinal curvature. Bracing is used in growing patients to stop a curve worsening; fusion surgery is generally reserved for curves projected to pass about 45 to 50 degrees.

Appearance concerns are one factor: Wikipedia notes visible changes can affect teenagers' quality of life and cosmetic concerns are a key reason adults choose surgery.
quick.mechanism: A rigid torso brace such as a TLSO applies corrective force while the spine grows. Fusion joins vertebrae with metal instrumentation and bone graft to correct and hold the curve.
quick.risks: Surgery can be painful with a months-long recovery, and full straightening is usually not possible. Brace effectiveness depends on compliance, and braces have caused skin irritation and low self-esteem.

lead: Bracing and spinal fusion are the two main established treatments for progressive scoliosis, a three-dimensional curvature of the spine that shows up as uneven shoulders, a prominent rib or shoulder blade, a leaning trunk or clothes that hang unevenly.[1][12] For a person with a curve, both treatments serve an appearance goal as well as a medical one: bracing is used while a patient is still growing to keep a curve from becoming larger and more visible, and fusion surgery straightens and holds the spine so the trunk looks more symmetrical.[1]

Bracing is used only while growth remains, with the aim of stopping the curve progressing to the point where surgery is recommended.[1] Surgery is usually recommended for curves likely to progress beyond about 45 to 50 degrees, for curves interfering with breathing or sitting, and for curves that would be cosmetically unacceptable in adulthood.[1] Wikipedia notes that cosmetic concerns are a key reason adults pursue surgery, and the NHS notes that scoliosis or wearing a brace can affect body image and self-esteem, particularly in children and teenagers.[1][12]

A large body of research surrounds both treatments, including a Scoliosis Research Society standardisation of brace-study criteria, electronic studies of how many hours braces are actually worn, discrete-choice studies of what patients prefer in a brace, trials of newer flexible and 3D-printed designs, and long-term outcome reviews of spinal fusion.[2][3][4][6][8][9][10] Wikipedia states that evidence shows bracing prevents curve progression, while its effect on quality of life, appearance or back pain is unclear.[1]

angle.text: Bracing aims to stop a growing teenager's curve getting larger, which limits visible asymmetry of the shoulders, ribs and waist. Fusion surgery corrects and fixes the curve with rods and bone graft, producing a straighter trunk; significant correction is typical although complete straightening is usually not possible.[1]

paras: Scoliosis is defined by most authorities, including the Scoliosis Research Society, as a curve of more than 10 degrees on the Cobb scale in the coronal plane, with a rotational component.[1][14] The most common form is adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, whose cause is unknown; Wikipedia estimates about 65 percent of cases are idiopathic, about 15 percent congenital and about 10 percent secondary to neuromuscular disease.[1] It most often appears around the pre-pubertal growth spurt and is diagnosed more often in girls.[1]

Wikipedia also reports that longitudinal studies of late-onset idiopathic scoliosis find little physical impairment other than back pain and cosmetic concerns, even when untreated, and cites a 50-year follow-up published in JAMA in 2003 finding that lifelong physical and mental health were comparable to the general population.[1] In that context the appearance of the trunk is one of the main factors people weigh when choosing between observation, bracing and surgery.

The Cobb angle, developed by the American orthopaedic surgeon John Robert Cobb, is the standard measurement: the angle between the upper endplate of the top vertebra and the lower endplate of the bottom vertebra of the curve on a standing X-ray. Bands used in descriptions are under 10 degrees (not scoliosis), 10 to 30 mild, 30 to 45 moderate and over 45 severe.[14] Measurements taken lying down read about 7 to 10 degrees lower than standing, and SOSORT uses a 45 to 50 degree surgical range because Cobb measurement carries roughly 5 degrees of error.[1][14]

Bracing criteria from the Scoliosis Research Society include curves progressing past 25 degrees, curves between 30 and 45 degrees, Risser sign 0 to 2 and under six months since menarche.[1] For growing patients, curves under 20 degrees are monitored, 20 to 29 degrees are managed according to risk factors, and curves over 30 degrees generally prompt a bracing recommendation.[1] The NHS says older children wear a back brace until they stop growing, and that a cast or plastic brace may be used in babies and toddlers.[12]

The most common brace is the thoracolumbar sacral orthosis (TLSO) such as the Boston brace, a custom-made fibreglass or plastic shell fitting from armpits to hips, typically worn 22 to 23 hours a day.[1] Night-only braces are more convenient but their effectiveness is uncertain.[1] The early Milwaukee brace, with metal rods attached to a girdle and extending to the neck, was associated with jaw and muscle pain, skin irritation and low self-esteem.[1] Wikipedia records that in some juvenile cases bracing has reduced curves substantially, for example from 40 to 18 degrees.[1]

A Scoliosis Research Society committee published standardised criteria for brace studies in 2005 after finding inconsistent inclusion criteria and definitions of effectiveness in earlier literature.[2] A prospective study of 34 subjects used a temperature sensor and logger embedded in a Wilmington brace to relate objectively measured wear time to curve progression, a link that had not previously been measured.[3] An electronic monitor called the Cricket was evaluated as a way to track brace wear.[4]

Research has examined how brace visual aesthetics affect user acceptance and compliance, which patients prefer in a brace in a discrete choice experiment, and which psychosocial characteristics predict whether adolescents wear the brace.[5][6][7] A review in Orthopedic Clinics of North America surveyed advances in brace treatment, and a workflow paper describes CAD/CAM adjustment of braces using 3D printing.[10][16]

Surgery uses anterior fusion through the chest wall, posterior fusion through the back with metal instrumentation, or both, and may take four to eight hours.[1] Bone graft, from the patient, a donor or synthetic, is placed between or beside the vertebrae and hardware holds the bones in position while they fuse into one segment.[17] Return to physical activity takes around six months, and full straightening is usually not possible although significant correction is typical.[1] The NHS describes surgery for children as sometimes controlling spinal growth, followed by a straightening operation once growth stops, and says surgery is needed in only a small number of cases.[12]

Risks listed for spinal fusion in general include blood loss, nerve injury, wound infection, blood clots, failure of the bones to fuse (pseudarthrosis), and adjacent segment disease, with smoking, vitamin D deficiency and osteoporosis raising risk.[17] A 1998 review of paediatric spinal deformity reported generally satisfactory long-term results of spinal fusion for idiopathic scoliosis and described the emergence of thoracoscopic endoscopic techniques.[18]

Before internal instrumentation, scoliosis patients had fusions without internal support that required months in plaster casts, and large curves could still worsen.[13] Paul Harrington, a professor of orthopaedic surgery at Baylor College of Medicine, developed his ratcheted stainless-steel distraction rod in 1953 with orthotist Thorkild Engen, and presented it at the 1958 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons meeting, where it met scepticism.[13] Zimmer produced it in the 1960s, Harrington appeared on a 1962 Time cover, and by Wikipedia's account up to a million people received Harrington rods before the late 1990s.[13] Fusion proved a required part of the procedure because unfused spines fatigued and broke the metal.[13]

The rods are associated with flatback syndrome in some patients, in which a rod extending into the lower spine fails to follow its natural curve; the same article notes it is not inevitable and many patients have had rods for decades without problems.[13] Two-rod systems with wires at each level followed in the 1970s and Cotrel-Dubousset three-dimensional instrumentation in the 1980s.[1]

The Schroth method was developed by Katharina Schroth (1894-1985), a German physiotherapist from Dresden who had scoliosis herself, was fitted with a steel brace at 16 and experimented on herself with mirrors, breathing patterns and a pulley system. She opened her first institute in Meissen in 1921 and a second in Sobernheim in 1955.[15] Its goals are de-rotating, elongating and stabilising the spine through muscular symmetry, rotational angular breathing and postural awareness.[15] A 2026 randomised controlled trial compared Schroth exercises with core training for early recovery after surgery for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.[19]

The Scoliosis Research Society brace-study standards, the Wilmington brace temperature-sensor study of 34 subjects, and the Cricket compliance monitor evaluation are the main published designs addressing how braces are worn and whether wear relates to outcome.[2][3][4] Registered trials include a randomised trial of a flexible thoracolumbar brace, trials of new and 3D-printed braces, a brace-treatment prevention trial of 170 participants, a brace-monitoring study of 87 participants and a trial of brace use for adult pain.[8][9][10][11][20][21] A study of surgical candidates examined predictors of back pain in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.[22]

For surgery, Wikipedia cites a Swedish randomised trial in lumbar stenosis, a different condition, finding no significant clinical benefit from adding fusion to decompression, and notes fusion evidence is mixed across indications.[17]

The NHS lists a visibly curved spine, uneven shoulders, a prominent hip or ribs and ill-fitting clothes as signs, and says scoliosis or wearing a back brace can affect body image and self-esteem.[12] Wikipedia notes that visible changes can significantly affect teenagers' quality of life and in extreme cases cause emotional stress.[1] Studies of brace aesthetics and of why adolescents do not wear braces examine this directly.[5][7]

Scoliosis is discussed in strength-training forums mainly as a back-health and lifting question, and surgery appears in threads about how fusions affect lifting. One T Nation poster describes discovering a lumbar curve at a check-up, and another links a manufacturer's patient page in a thread about a back that looks uneven.[23][24]

lore.intro: Forum discussion of scoliosis treatment is sparse and mostly concerns how curves and surgery affect lifting and appearance.[23][24]

claims.claim: Bracing can prevent a curve from needing surgery.
claims.believers: Patients and clinicians who recommend bracing say it holds a growing teenager's curve below the surgical range.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states evidence shows bracing prevents curve progression, with effect on appearance and back pain unclear, and compliance research relates wear time to results.[1][3]

claims.claim: Surgery can fully straighten the spine.
claims.believers: Some patients hope for a completely straight back after fusion.
claims.experts: Wikipedia states that completely straightening a scoliotic spine is usually not possible, though significant correction is typical.[1]

claims.claim: Exercise methods such as Schroth can correct curves.
claims.believers: Schroth's own approach aims to de-rotate, elongate and stabilise the spine through breathing and postural work.[15]
claims.experts: Trials compare Schroth with other exercise in specific settings such as post-surgical recovery.[19]

claims.claim: Fusion surgery limits later lifting and sport.
claims.believers: Lifters on T Nation describe fusions and the need to be careful with weights afterwards.[24]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports return to physical activity after scoliosis surgery takes around six months.[1]

claims.claim: Untreated scoliosis always progresses to disability.
claims.believers: Older assumptions held that untreated curves would lead to cardiopulmonary disability.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that long-term studies of idiopathic scoliosis found health comparable to the general population, with back pain and cosmetic concerns the main issues.[1]
